strings.name: Rishi Sunak
strings.role: Former UK prime minister and Conservative MP
strings.summary: Rishi Sunak is a British Conservative politician who served as chancellor of the Exchequer from 2020 to 2022 and prime minister from 2022 to 2024. His career includes pandemic employment support, post-Brexit arrangements for Northern Ireland and legal disputes over migration policy. After leaving Downing Street, he remained an MP and took corporate advisory roles, distinct from government office.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026. Parliamentary records establish current and former offices; Hansard records an actual contribution on 12 November. Policy announcements, court decisions and implementation are distinguished.
strings.influence.rationale: A former UK prime minister and chancellor, involved in pandemic fiscal support, responses to inflation and the United Kingdom’s external economic policy.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Southampton on 12 May 1980. He entered Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1998 and graduated in 2001 with a first-class degree in philosophy, politics and economics. He subsequently earned an MBA at Stanford as a Fulbright scholar, graduating in 2006.
strings.facts.f2.label: From finance to politics
strings.facts.f2.value: Before politics he worked at Goldman Sachs and The Children’s Investment Fund and co-founded an investment firm. Entering the Commons in 2015, he later held posts as a local-government junior minister, chief secretary to the Treasury and chancellor. Since 2024 he has represented Richmond and Northallerton.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Constituency work after Downing Street
strings.highlights.h1.text: On 12 November 2026 he raised the shortage of parking at Northallerton station in the Commons, saying he had convened the council, mayor’s office and rail operator and sought clarity on transport grants. Hansard records the question; it does not establish that funding or construction was approved.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Disclosed corporate advisory roles
strings.highlights.h2.text: The members’ interests register lists his senior advisory roles at Anthropic and Microsoft as starting on 9 October 2025. These are disclosed outside jobs, not ministerial appointments; role commencement, remuneration agreements and registration dates may differ.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Leaves the premiership and leads the opposition
strings.timeline.t1.text: His premiership ended and he became leader of the official opposition in the Commons. That post and his Conservative leadership both ended on 2 November. He retained a parliamentary seat by winning Richmond and Northallerton under the new boundaries in the 4 July general election.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Supreme Court rejects the Rwanda removal policy
strings.timeline.t2.text: The court unanimously upheld the finding that the policy was unlawful, identifying a real risk of asylum seekers being returned to their home countries and ill-treated under the arrangements then in place. The ruling concerned that policy and evidence, not a criminal conviction of Sunak, and does not replace analysis of later legislation.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Announces the Windsor Framework agreement
strings.timeline.t3.text: With European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, he announced an agreement changing how the Northern Ireland Protocol operated, covering goods, taxation and regulation. Legal and Joint Committee processes still followed the political agreement; announcement did not mean every measure was already in force.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Becomes UK prime minister
strings.timeline.t4.text: After becoming Conservative leader on 24 October, he took office as prime minister the following day. The party leadership transition and government appointment were separate events, not a new general-election victory.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Announces the pandemic job retention scheme
strings.timeline.t5.text: As chancellor he announced grants to employers for staff temporarily not working but retained on payroll, initially covering 80% of wages up to £2,500 a month, backdated to 1 March. Announcement, opening applications and actual payments were separate events.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes chancellor of the Exchequer
strings.timeline.t6.text: Promoted from chief secretary to the Treasury, he held responsibility for fiscal and economic policy until 5 July 2022. He introduced support during the pandemic; budget allocations and actual economic effects require separate assessment.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes chief secretary to the Treasury
strings.timeline.t7.text: He left the junior ministerial post in Housing, Communities and Local Government held since 9 January 2018 and became chief secretary, serving until 13 February 2020. He was not yet chancellor or prime minister.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First elected to the Commons
strings.timeline.t8.text: He won Richmond (Yorks) as a Conservative. Parliamentary records show three elections in that former constituency; its name is distinguished from the seat created under the 2024 boundaries.
